landing.faq.stack.question: What's the tech stack?
landing.faq.stack.answer: Next.js 16 with the App Router, React 19, TypeScript strict mode, Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, Drizzle ORM, and better-auth. Every piece of business logic is inlined — no external packages for payment, email, storage, or AI.
landing.faq.payment.question: Which payment providers are supported?
landing.faq.payment.answer: Stripe, PayPal, Creem, Alipay, and WeChat Pay out of the box. The PaymentManager abstraction makes it straightforward to add more providers by implementing a single interface.
landing.faq.database.question: Which databases can I use?
landing.faq.database.answer: Drizzle ORM handles PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Turso, and Cloudflare D1. Switch providers by editing DATABASE_PROVIDER in your .env — the schema templates and drizzle config adapt automatically.
landing.faq.customize.question: How customizable is the landing page?
landing.faq.customize.answer: The src/blocks/ directory ships with demo sections — they're designed to be rewritten per project. The durable primitives live in src/components/, so your rebrand touches blocks and translations, not the chassis.
landing.faq.license.question: Can I use this for commercial projects?
landing.faq.license.answer: Yes. ShipAny Next is built for shipping production SaaS products. You own the code after cloning — no per-seat fees, no runtime dependencies on our infrastructure.
landing.cta.headline: Ready to ship your SaaS?
landing.cta.subheadline: Stop wiring auth, payments, and RBAC from scratch. Start with ShipAny Next and build what actually makes your product unique.

music.learning.intro: Start with five notes, build a melody, and find your rhythm. Short, hands-on lessons turn the keyboard into a place you feel at home.
music.learning.courseTitle: From your first note to your first melody
music.learning.lesson1.title: Meet middle C
music.learning.lesson1.desc: Find your starting point and play your first five notes.
music.learning.lesson1.body: Look for the group of two black keys. C is the white key immediately to their left. The C near the center of a full piano is middle C (C4). Rest your right thumb on C4, index finger on D4, and middle finger on E4. Keep your wrist relaxed and gently curved fingers close to the keys. Play C–D–E–D–C, one note at a time. Notice how moving right raises the pitch and moving left lowers it.
music.learning.lesson1.tip: On a real piano: thumb = 1, index = 2, middle = 3. Use 1–2–3–2–1. On screen, tap the same notes below.
music.learning.lesson2.title: Play a familiar melody
music.learning.lesson2.desc: Turn three notes into the opening of a nursery melody.
music.learning.lesson2.body: A melody is a sequence of pitches with a shape you can sing. Here is the opening phrase of Mary Had a Little Lamb: E–D–C–D–E–E–E. Put your right-hand fingers 1, 2, and 3 on C4, D4, and E4. Begin with finger 3, move down to 2 and 1, then climb back up. Repeated notes need a gentle release between presses. Play slowly enough that each change feels deliberate; speed can wait.
music.learning.lesson2.tip: Suggested fingers: 3–2–1–2–3–3–3. Hold the final E for two counts. First learn the pitches, then sing and play together.
music.learning.lesson3.title: Find a steady pulse
music.learning.lesson3.desc: Feel quarter notes and half notes at 80 beats per minute.
music.learning.lesson3.body: A steady pulse is the clock underneath your music. At 80 beats per minute, each beat lasts three quarters of a second. A quarter note occupies one beat; a half note occupies two. Listen to the example, then play C–C–E–E–G. Leave one beat between the first two changes and two beats between the next changes: 1, 1, 2, 2. This exercise checks when you start each note, not how long you hold a screen key.
music.learning.lesson3.tip: Count out loud: C (1), C (2), E (3–4), E (1–2), G (3–4). The checker allows a little timing flexibility; a restart gives you a fresh attempt.
music.learning.lesson4.title: Bring in your left hand
music.learning.lesson4.desc: Build the sound of a C major chord, one note at a time.
music.learning.lesson4.body: Move one octave below middle C to C3. Your left-hand little finger rests on C3, middle finger on E3, and thumb on G3. These are the three notes of a C major chord. Playing them separately makes a broken chord, a simple accompaniment pattern. Try C3–E3–G3–E3–C3. Let your hand remain soft and avoid stretching farther than feels comfortable. Later, this pattern can support a right-hand melody.
music.learning.lesson4.tip: Suggested left-hand fingers: 5–3–1–3–5. Learn this hand separately before combining it with a melody. Use the chord finder to explore more shapes.

sf.editorial.home.title: Music notes, from a first look to a familiar language
sf.editorial.home.intro: Read the position. Find the key. Hear the connection. These small steps turn the symbols on a page into something you can actually play.
sf.editorial.home.start.title: What a music note tells you
sf.editorial.home.start.p0: A written music note combines two useful instructions: which pitch to play and how long to hold it. Its position on the staff tells you the pitch, once you know the clef. Its shape tells you a relative duration. Begin by separating those jobs. You can learn to recognize a note without also solving a complicated rhythm at the same time.
sf.editorial.home.start.p1: In the trainer, look at the center of the notehead. Is a staff line running through it, or is it sitting in a space? That distinction matters more than the direction of the stem. A stem pointing up and a stem pointing down can represent the same pitch. Read the notehead first, then use the keyboard to connect that position with a sound.
sf.editorial.home.start.p2: A label such as C4 includes both a letter and an octave number. The letter identifies the note family; the number distinguishes this C from the many other Cs on a piano. C4 means middle C in scientific pitch notation. For a beginner, noticing the octave prevents a common mistake: choosing a correctly named key in the wrong register and wondering why the result sounds different.
sf.editorial.home.map.title: Find your way around the keyboard
sf.editorial.home.map.p0: The musical alphabet runs A, B, C, D, E, F, G, then begins again. On the piano, moving right usually means moving higher in pitch; moving left means lower. The white keys repeat the same seven letters. You do not need to memorize the entire keyboard at once. Learn one group, then notice that the pattern repeats across the instrument.
sf.editorial.home.map.p1: Use the black keys as landmarks. They appear in alternating groups of two and three. C is the white key immediately to the left of a group of two black keys. F is immediately to the left of a group of three. Once you locate C, walk along the white keys to find D, E, F, G, A, and B before reaching the next C.
sf.editorial.home.map.p2: Black keys belong to the same pitch system. The key between C and D can be called C-sharp or D-flat, depending on the notation and musical context. Start with the white keys if you are learning staff positions, then add sharps and flats. There is no black key between E and F or between B and C; these neighboring white keys are already a semitone apart.
sf.editorial.home.recognize.title: Read from landmarks, then recognize patterns
sf.editorial.home.recognize.p0: A clef fixes the meaning of the staff. In treble clef, the second line from the bottom is G4. In bass clef, the second line from the top is F3. These are useful anchor notes. Identify the clef before guessing a letter: the same visual position on two different clefs does not normally mean the same pitch. One quick check can prevent an entire chain of mistakes.
sf.editorial.home.recognize.p1: From a known note, move one letter for every neighboring line or space. A step from a line to the next space moves to the next letter. A move from one line to the next line skips a letter and forms a third. Practice seeing those distances. Counting from the bottom of the staff every time works, but eventually slows you down when a melody has many notes.
sf.editorial.home.recognize.p2: Combine memory and movement. First recognize a landmark such as middle C, treble G, or bass F. Then describe the next note as one step above or a third below. When the same position comes back several times, try naming it directly. This approach helps you read both an isolated note in a quiz and a sequence in real music, where neighboring notes provide valuable clues.
sf.editorial.home.connect.title: Use the trainer and explorer for different jobs
sf.editorial.home.connect.p0: In a note drill, commit to an answer before revealing it. Look at the clef, name the letter and octave, then choose the matching key. Immediate feedback is useful because you can compare your reasoning with the correct position while the question is still fresh. If you miss a note, find one nearby landmark and explain the distance to yourself before continuing.
sf.editorial.home.connect.p1: The keyboard explorer reverses that process: select a key and inspect where its note appears on the staff. Use it when a position feels unfamiliar, or compare the same pitch under different clefs. This is exploration rather than a scored test. Play adjacent white keys slowly and watch the notehead alternate between lines and spaces; the movement makes the abstract alphabet much easier to understand.
sf.editorial.home.connect.p2: Sound adds another connection, but it does not replace reading. Listen to the selected key after you have identified its notation. Ask whether the pitch moved up, down, or stayed the same. Keep the volume comfortable and take your time. A virtual keyboard is enough for this recognition exercise, although a physical piano will eventually add finger movement, touch, and coordination to the task.
sf.editorial.home.practice.title: Make a short session count
sf.editorial.home.practice.p0: Choose one small goal for each session, such as recognizing the five treble lines or finding every C in the displayed range. Spend a minute exploring those positions, then answer a short set without help. Read the result as information about what to revisit. A high score on familiar notes is encouraging, but a lower score on a new clef can still represent useful learning.
sf.editorial.home.practice.p1: After a mistake, avoid immediately pressing random keys until the feedback turns positive. Say the correct note, locate it again, and compare it with your original answer. Were you one staff position away, using the wrong clef, or an octave too high? Naming the type of error gives your next attempt a purpose and makes practice more productive than simply repeating the same number of questions.
sf.editorial.home.practice.p2: Finish by reading a tiny pattern away from the quiz: C–D–E–D–C, for example. Name the notes, find them on the keyboard, and play them with an even pulse. When letter names feel comfortable, move to the dedicated treble or bass trainer for a wider range. The reading guide introduces note lengths and meter so that these separate pitches can begin to sound like a phrase.
sf.editorial.treble.title: Make the treble staff feel familiar
sf.editorial.treble.intro: Learn the reference points first, then read the spaces between them. A few dependable landmarks are more useful than a hurried guess.
sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.title: Begin with the G-clef landmark
sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p0: Treble clef is also called the G clef. Its curl centers on the second staff line from the bottom, identifying that line as G4. From there, the other lines and spaces follow the musical alphabet. Check this landmark whenever you begin a new exercise. The clef is part of the instruction, not a decorative symbol you can ignore once the notes appear.
sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p1: The treble staff commonly represents music in a higher register, including much right-hand piano writing. It is also used by many other instruments and voices. It does not mean that every note must be played with the right hand. A piano score can change clefs when the range changes, and fingering or hand distribution is a separate decision from identifying the written pitch.
sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p2: Build three starting points: middle C on its short ledger line below the staff, G4 on the second line, and C5 in the third space. Find each on the keyboard, then return to the staff. These anchors divide the range into smaller neighborhoods. Instead of counting a long distance from the bottom, you can start with whichever known note lies closest to the question.
sf.editorial.treble.lines.title: Learn lines and spaces in order
sf.editorial.treble.lines.p0: Read treble lines from bottom to top as E4, G4, B4, D5, and F5. The familiar phrase Every Good Boy Does Fine can help recall E–G–B–D–F. Use any sentence that you remember easily, but keep its direction clear. Starting at the top reverses the sequence. A mnemonic is a temporary memory aid, not a rule about how melodies must move.
sf.editorial.treble.lines.p1: The four spaces, also read from bottom to top, spell F4, A4, C5, and E5: FACE. Notice that the lines and spaces interleave. Beginning on the bottom line, the complete sequence is E4, F4, G4, A4, B4, C5, D5, E5, F5. Practice that combined sequence so that you do not treat line notes and space notes as two unrelated systems.
sf.editorial.treble.lines.p2: Look at the notehead rather than the stem or flag. A note on the middle line is B4 whether its stem points upward or downward. If the notehead is centered between two lines, it belongs to that space even when its stem crosses several others. Slowing down to locate the notehead accurately is usually more helpful than repeating a mnemonic faster under pressure.
sf.editorial.treble.ledger.title: Read beyond the five lines
sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p0: Ledger lines extend the staff when a pitch is too low or high to fit comfortably inside it. Middle C, or C4, sits on the first ledger line below the treble staff. D4 occupies the space between that ledger line and the bottom staff line. E4 is on the bottom line itself. Learn this three-note doorway as one connected pattern rather than three separate facts.
sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p1: Above the staff, G5 sits in the space immediately above the top line, and A5 is on the first ledger line above it. The alphabet continues without a new rule. Each move to the next line or space advances one letter. Count the spaces as well as the short lines; counting only ledger lines makes it easy to skip a note and answer a third too high.
sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p2: Octave numbers help distinguish repeated letters across this range. C4 and C5 are both C, but they are different keys and different sounds. The number changes when B moves up to C, so B4 is followed by C5. If the trainer expects a specific pitch, check both parts of the name. A correct letter in the wrong octave is a useful clue about a register-reading mistake.
sf.editorial.treble.patterns.title: Turn single notes into melodic shapes
sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p0: Once you can find individual pitches, begin reading how they relate. E4–F4–G4 moves upward by steps, alternating line, space, line. E4–G4–B4 moves upward by thirds, staying on lines. You can often see those patterns before naming every note. Find the first pitch carefully, then follow the shape while checking the names. This makes the staff feel like a map of movement.
sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p1: Repeated notes deserve attention too. Several identical noteheads in a row keep the same pitch even if their rhythms differ. A melody can also return to a familiar position after a leap. Scan a short phrase for repetitions before playing it. Grouping repeated material reduces the number of new decisions you need to make and leaves more attention available for rhythm and a steady pulse.
sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p2: Sharps, flats, and naturals modify a written pitch without moving its letter position on the staff. F-sharp is still written on an F line or space, with an accidental or key signature supplying the alteration. When you begin working with accidentals, identify the letter first and then apply the symbol. This two-step method prevents confusing a black piano key with an entirely new staff position.
sf.editorial.treble.practice.title: A focused treble-clef routine
sf.editorial.treble.practice.p0: Start a session by locating G4, C5, and middle C without a hint. Then practice a small group around one landmark, such as E4 through A4. Expand the range only when those positions feel dependable. Mixing every possible pitch immediately can make it difficult to tell whether the problem is a single unfamiliar note, ledger-line counting, or simply too many new positions at once.
sf.editorial.treble.practice.p1: Use the answer reveal as a teaching step after making a real attempt. Compare the correct position with the one you expected, then say the note name before choosing the next question. Keep track of the notes you confuse, especially neighboring line and space positions. On the next session, explore those pairs on the keyboard before testing them again. Deliberate correction matters more than protecting a streak.
sf.editorial.treble.practice.p2: Finally, read a five-note melody at a comfortable speed, keeping the pulse even enough to continue through a small hesitation. You might use C4–D4–E4–D4–C4 with one equal-length note per pulse. When this becomes easy, change the rhythm or starting note, but not both at once. Explore bass clef next to understand how the other half of a piano score connects to the same keyboard.
sf.editorial.bass.title: Read bass notes with a clear sense of direction
sf.editorial.bass.intro: The lower staff follows the same alphabet. New landmarks help you read it on its own terms and connect it to the whole piano.
sf.editorial.bass.orientation.title: What the bass clef actually changes
sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p0: Bass clef assigns a different set of pitches to the staff than treble clef does. Its two dots sit on either side of the second line from the top, marking that line as F3. That is why it is also called the F clef. Begin every bass exercise by noticing those dots. Reading a bass note with a memorized treble pattern produces the wrong pitch.
sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p1: The bass staff is useful for lower music: bass voices, instruments such as cello and bassoon, and many left-hand piano parts. Lower register does not mean simpler music. A bass line can carry a melody, establish a chord, or create a rhythmic pattern. Learning to read it independently gives you access to musical information that is easy to miss when you focus only on a tune above it.
sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p2: On a piano, the staff does not permanently belong to a particular hand. The left hand often plays bass-clef material, but clefs describe pitch ranges, not fingers. Keep these ideas separate while practicing. First identify the written pitch and locate its key. Later, use the score, fingering, and musical context to decide which hand should play it and how to move comfortably between notes.
sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.title: Use F3, the spaces, and the lines
sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p0: Bass-clef lines from bottom to top are G2, B2, D3, F3, and A3. A common memory phrase is Good Boys Do Fine Always. The four spaces are A2, C3, E3, and G3, often remembered as All Cows Eat Grass. Say the letters as well as the sentence. The goal is to recognize G2 or C3 directly, rather than mentally reciting a whole phrase for every note.
sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p1: Use F3 as your central anchor because the clef itself points to it. One staff step below is E3 in a space; one step above is G3 in a space. D3 lies on the middle line. Those neighboring pitches give you a compact region to practice first. Play D3–E3–F3–G3 slowly while watching the noteheads alternate between lines and spaces on the display.
sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p2: Another useful reference is C3 in the second space from the bottom. Compare it with middle C, C4, above the staff: the letters match but the octave differs. Finding both on a keyboard helps prevent treating every C as the same key. When a question feels difficult, identify a nearby landmark and count individual lines and spaces outward instead of restarting from the lowest staff line.
sf.editorial.bass.register.title: Connect ledger lines and middle C
sf.editorial.bass.register.p0: Middle C is written on the first ledger line above the bass staff. Immediately below it, B3 sits in the space above the top line, and A3 sits on that top line. This A3–B3–C4 sequence is a useful bridge toward treble clef. Middle C below a treble staff and middle C above a bass staff represent exactly the same piano key, not two neighboring Cs.
sf.editorial.bass.register.p1: Below the bass staff, F2 sits in the space beneath the bottom line and E2 lies on the first ledger line below it. Continue downward through the alphabet in reverse: E, D, C, B, A, G, F. Octave numbers decrease when you move down from C to B. For example, descending from C3 leads to B2, not B3. This is notation for register, not a change in the alphabet itself.
sf.editorial.bass.register.p2: The grand staff joins treble and bass staves with a brace in many piano scores. Think of it as two readable windows into one continuous pitch range. Notes written above bass and below treble can overlap, because the choice of clef also serves readability. Do not assume that the empty printed gap between the staves represents a special musical interval; spacing on the page can change.
sf.editorial.bass.patterns.title: See the shape of a bass line
sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p0: Bass parts often become easier when you recognize intervals rather than isolated letters. A line-to-next-line movement is a third; a line-to-neighboring-space movement is a step. Try C3–E3–G3, the notes of a C major triad. All three occupy spaces in bass clef. Notice their visual shape, then compare it with D3–F3–A3 on lines. The distances look alike even though the notes differ.
sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p1: An accompaniment may alternate a low root note with a chord, or move between a root and its fifth. Before playing, identify repeated pitches and recurring shapes. You still need to read accidentals and rhythm, but recognizing the pattern gives the passage some structure. Avoid assuming that every low note is the root of the current chord; inversions and moving bass lines can put other chord tones underneath.
sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p2: Read vertically as well as horizontally when several noteheads are stacked. They normally sound together as a chord rather than as a fast sequence. Name the lowest pitch first, then inspect the intervals above it. If the span is unfamiliar, use the keyboard explorer to hear the notes separately before combining them. This keeps the reading task clear while you build the coordination needed to play them together.
sf.editorial.bass.practice.title: Build accuracy before adding hand movement
sf.editorial.bass.practice.p0: Practice bass clef by itself for part of your session, even if your treble reading is already comfortable. Begin with F3, D3, and C3, then add their neighbors. Naming a pitch aloud and selecting its key is enough at first. You do not need to play a difficult left-hand pattern while also learning the note positions. Separating these demands makes the source of a mistake easier to see.
sf.editorial.bass.practice.p1: When you miss an answer, check three things in order: the clef, the line or space, and the octave. If you repeatedly answer with a treble name, spend a minute returning to the F3 landmark. If the letter is right but the register is wrong, compare the two matching letter names on the keyboard. Use the result to choose the next practice target rather than simply restarting the score.
sf.editorial.bass.practice.p2: End with a small musical task, such as reading C3–G2–C3–E3 with equal note lengths. Keep the pulse slow and listen to the direction of each move. Later, combine one bass note with a simple treble melody to connect both staves. The piano chord finder can help you hear how a low note supports harmony, while the reading guide adds the rhythmic symbols needed for complete phrases.
sf.editorial.chords.title: Understand the notes behind every piano chord
sf.editorial.chords.intro: Choose a root, compare a chord quality, and listen closely. The useful part is discovering why a small change in notes creates a different sound.
sf.editorial.chords.formula.title: Build a chord from a root and a formula
sf.editorial.chords.formula.p0: A chord combines notes that are heard together, or understood together when played in sequence. A basic triad uses three different note names: a root, a third, and a fifth. The root gives the chord its name. In C major, C is the root, E is the third, and G is the fifth. These names describe relationships to C, not fixed locations on the keyboard.
sf.editorial.chords.formula.p1: The finder turns that relationship into visible keys. Select a root note, choose the chord type, then find the result. Read the note names before playing the sound. Comparing the keyboard highlights with the labels helps you understand the chord as a set of pitches rather than a hand shape to memorize. You can build the same quality from another root by preserving the distances between its notes.
sf.editorial.chords.formula.p2: Those distances can be measured in semitones, the smallest steps between neighboring piano keys. Count both black and white keys. From C to C-sharp is one semitone, and from E to F is also one. A major triad places notes at zero, four, and seven semitones above the root. Count movements rather than counting the starting key as one, otherwise every interval will be one step short.
sf.editorial.chords.quality.title: Hear what changes between chord types
sf.editorial.chords.quality.p0: A minor triad uses zero, three, and seven semitones above its root. Compare C major, C–E–G, with C minor, C–E-flat–G. Only the third changes, yet the color of the chord shifts. Major and minor are structural labels; they are not guarantees that a passage must sound happy or sad. Tempo, register, rhythm, and the surrounding harmony all influence how a listener experiences the result.
sf.editorial.chords.quality.p1: A dominant seventh chord adds a minor seventh to a major triad: C7 contains C, E, G, and B-flat. A major seventh chord uses B-natural instead, so Cmaj7 is C, E, G, B. These symbols are not interchangeable. Listen to them back to back with the same root and register. Concentrating on the changed upper note makes the distinction easier to hear than comparing two unrelated chords.
sf.editorial.chords.quality.p2: Suspended chords replace the third. Csus4 contains C, F, and G, while Csus2 contains C, D, and G. Without E or E-flat, neither is a standard major or minor triad. Diminished and augmented triads change the fifth as well: C diminished uses C, E-flat, G-flat, and C augmented uses C, E, G-sharp. Introduce these types one at a time and describe which key moved between examples.
sf.editorial.chords.inversions.title: Keep the chord, change the lowest note
sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p0: An inversion rearranges a chord so a note other than the root becomes the lowest pitch. C–E–G is root-position C major. E–G–C is its first inversion, and G–C–E is its second inversion. The set of note names remains C, E, and G. Use the inversion control to compare these arrangements and listen to how a different bass note changes the weight of the same harmony.
sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p1: A slash symbol can name the bass explicitly. C/E means a C major chord with E in the bass; it does not mean a C chord followed by an E chord. This is useful when reading a song chart because the bass line may move while the harmony stays closely related. Check the lowest highlighted key in the finder, then identify the remaining chord tones above it.
sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p2: Finger numbers describe a suggested hand position, not the definition of a chord. Piano fingers are numbered one through five from thumb to little finger on either hand. A comfortable fingering depends on hand size, register, inversion, and the notes before and after the chord. Treat a displayed fingering as a starting point. Avoid forcing a stretch; you can practice the pitches separately while deciding on a comfortable movement.
sf.editorial.chords.progressions.title: Listen to chords as a sequence
sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p0: A progression is an ordered series of chords. C–G–Am–F uses C major, G major, A minor, and F major. In the key of C major, these are commonly labeled I–V–vi–IV. The numerals describe scale-degree roots and chord quality, making it possible to recognize the same pattern in another key. Uppercase numerals here indicate major triads; the lowercase vi indicates a minor triad.
sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p1: Compare that sequence with G–D–Em–C. It follows I–V–vi–IV in G major, so the relationships are similar although the pitches have moved. Play each progression at a steady pace, then sing or hum the bass roots if comfortable. Listen for the change from one chord to the next rather than trying to label each sound as an emotion. Context is part of what makes harmony interesting.
sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p2: Inversions can make a progression easier to play by keeping neighboring chords close together. For example, C–E–G can move to B–D–G for a G chord with B in the bass. The top G stays in place while the other voices move downward. This is a simple example of voice leading. Explore nearby notes before assuming that every new chord must be played in root position with a large hand jump.
sf.editorial.chords.practice.title: Practice a useful comparison, not a long list
sf.editorial.chords.practice.p0: Choose one root and compare major, minor, and suspended fourth chords. Before listening, predict which note should change. Then check the highlights and say the complete set of note names. This turns the finder into an active exercise. If you only press play repeatedly, the sounds may become familiar without building the ability to construct a chord when you encounter its symbol on a new chart.
sf.editorial.chords.practice.p1: Next, build the same chord quality on a different root. Remember that black keys can have different written names depending on context. D-flat and C-sharp share a piano key in standard equal temperament, but correct chord spelling still follows the letter relationships of the formula. In a D major triad, the third is F-sharp, not G-flat, because D to F uses the letter distance of a third.
sf.editorial.chords.practice.p2: Finish with two or four chords and a slow pulse. Play each as a block, then as separate notes, keeping the total time for each chord consistent. If a change is awkward, practice just that transition before returning to the full sequence. The music notes trainers strengthen the staff-to-key connection, and the reading guide explains note values so you can turn chord symbols and highlighted keys into a timed musical part.

sf.editorial.guide.title: Your first steps into written music
sf.editorial.guide.intro: You do not have to understand every symbol before making a start. Reading music is a collection of smaller skills: locating pitches, following durations, keeping a pulse, and noticing expression. Learn one layer, try it, then connect it to the next. This guide begins with the staff and ends with a practical routine you can repeat. A virtual keyboard is enough for the early examples. When you sit at a physical instrument, bring the same patient approach and choose a short passage with only a few new ideas.
sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.title: What is sheet music?
sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p0: Sheet music is a written way to communicate musical sounds and their timing. In standard staff notation, symbols show pitches, durations, silences, and expressive instructions. Read most music from left to right; notes aligned vertically often happen together. A score can contain a single melody or several parts that coordinate different performers. You do not need to hear a recording first to begin interpreting it, although listening can help you connect the symbols with the result. Think of the page as a set of relationships to understand, rather than a picture of finger movements that you must copy exactly.
sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p1: Reading offers three practical benefits. First, it lets you approach music you have not memorized or heard repeatedly. Second, it helps you communicate: you can point to a measure, a note, or a rhythm when practicing with someone else. Third, it makes musical patterns visible. You can see where a melody repeats, where a chord changes, and how a phrase is organized. None of this makes playing by ear less valuable. Reading, listening, improvising, and remembering reinforce one another, so there is no need to choose one permanent learning identity before you start making music.
sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p2: Before playing a page, take a brief survey. Find the clef at the beginning of each staff, the key signature if one appears, and the time signature. Look for the first note and any repeat signs. If there are two joined staves, notice which events line up. In this guide, you will first learn where notes live, then how their shapes organize time, and finally how rests and dynamics shape expression. Use the contents links to revisit one idea, and try the small examples before moving on. Accurate, comfortable reading begins with understanding a manageable amount of information.
sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.title: The staff and clefs
sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p0: A staff has five horizontal lines and four spaces. Count both from the bottom upward. A notehead can sit on a line, with the line passing through its center, or in a space between two lines. Moving to the next line or space moves one letter through the musical alphabet. The clef tells you which pitches those positions represent. Without checking it, a beautifully counted staff position may still produce the wrong answer. Start with the notehead rather than its stem: stem direction helps the notation fit together visually, but does not independently change a note's pitch.
sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p1: Treble clef identifies G4 on the second line from the bottom. Its five lines are E4, G4, B4, D5, and F5. Remember E–G–B–D–F with Every Good Boy Does Fine, or another sentence you like. Its spaces spell FACE: F4, A4, C5, and E5. A mnemonic can get you started, but practice finding notes directly as well. For example, locate G4 using the clef, then move one position upward to A4 and one downward to F4. These nearby relationships will later help you read melodies more smoothly than reciting a sentence for every pitch.
sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p2: Bass clef identifies F3 on the second line from the top, between the symbol's two dots. From bottom to top its lines are G2, B2, D3, F3, and A3; its spaces are A2, C3, E3, and G3. Good Boys Do Fine Always and All Cows Eat Grass are common memory aids. Notice that bass clef is not treble clef played vaguely lower: each written position has a specific meaning. Practice F3 and its neighbors until you can locate them without converting from a treble-clef answer in your head. Treat bass reading as its own useful skill.
sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p3: Ledger lines are short extensions used for notes outside the staff. Middle C, C4, sits on the first ledger line below treble clef and the first ledger line above bass clef. Both symbols mean the same key. In the explorer, switch clefs while keeping the pitch fixed and watch its written position change. The sound stays the same because a clef changes the map, not the pitch you selected. Try D4 next: it sits in the space below the treble staff and above the middle-C ledger line in bass clef. Count every line and space, including those outside the staff.
sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.title: Note names and the musical alphabet
sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p0: Music uses seven letter names, A through G, which repeat in ascending order. Starting on C gives C, D, E, F, G, A, B, then another C. The distance between these two Cs is an octave. Scientific pitch notation adds a number so you can distinguish registers: middle C is C4, and the C an octave above is C5. The number changes at C, so B3 is immediately below C4. This labeling is especially useful on a virtual keyboard, where you may see only part of the instrument and cannot rely on a full piano's physical center to orient yourself.
sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p1: On the keyboard, locate the repeating groups of two and three black keys. C is just to the left of a two-black-key group; F is just to the left of a three-black-key group. Move right along the white keys from C and say the alphabet aloud. Then move back left, reversing the names. Do not skip from G straight to a new C: A and B come between them. On the staff, the same sequence climbs through alternating lines and spaces. Select neighboring keys in the explorer and watch that movement, then try predicting the next written position before you press it.
sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p2: A sharp raises a written note by one semitone, a flat lowers it by one semitone, and a natural cancels a prior alteration where applicable. On a piano, a semitone is the distance to the next key, black or white. E–F and B–C are semitones even though both keys are white. C-sharp and D-flat share a key in standard equal temperament, but the spelling depends on musical context. A key signature applies its listed sharps or flats throughout the music until changed; a local accidental normally applies to the same written pitch through the remainder of its measure. Begin with natural notes, then add these symbols deliberately.
sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.title: Note values and rhythm
sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p0: Pitch answers which note; rhythm answers when and for how long. A note's shape gives its duration relative to other notes. A whole note equals two half notes, four quarter notes, eight eighth notes, or sixteen sixteenth notes. These are ratios, not fixed seconds. In a passage where the quarter note receives one beat, a half note lasts two beats and a whole note lasts four. The tempo decides how quickly those beats pass. At a quarter-note tempo of 60 beats per minute, each quarter-note beat lasts one second; at 120, it lasts half a second.
sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p1: Notice the visual differences. A whole note has an open notehead without a stem. A half note adds a stem; a quarter note fills the head. Eighth notes add one flag, and sixteenth notes add two. When grouped, beams replace the flags without changing the durations. Keep a steady pulse while saying one-and, two-and to divide each quarter-note beat into two eighth notes. For sixteenth notes, one-e-and-a divides it into four. The syllables are a counting aid; the important part is spacing each subdivision evenly instead of rushing the smaller notes.
sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p2: A dot adds half of the original note value. A dotted half note equals three quarter notes; a dotted quarter equals three eighth notes. A tie joins notes of the same pitch into one continuous sound with their durations added. For example, a quarter tied to an eighth lasts one and a half quarter-note beats. Play the first note and continue holding through the second symbol without striking it again. A slur may look similar but generally groups different pitches into a phrase or articulation. Check whether the curved line connects identical pitches before interpreting it as a tie.
sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p3: Try a rhythm before adding pitch. In 4/4, clap a half note followed by two quarter notes: clap on beat one, keep holding through beat two, then clap on three and four. Next replace the final quarter with two eighth notes, clapping four-and. Count aloud through the held notes instead of going silent mentally. If the pulse becomes uneven, slow down and repeat one measure. Then play the same rhythm on a single piano key. Adding a melody is a later step; a rhythm that feels clear on one note is much easier to keep steady while reading several pitches.
sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.title: Time signatures and measures
sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p0: Barlines divide music into measures, also called bars. The time signature near the beginning describes how durations are grouped. In simple meters such as 4/4 and 3/4, the top number gives the number of beats in a measure, and the bottom number identifies the note value for a beat. Four on the bottom means a quarter note. Count 4/4 as one, two, three, four, and 3/4 as one, two, three. Restart the count after the barline while keeping time continuous. A barline organizes the music; it does not automatically tell you to pause or lift your hands.
sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p1: Compound meter needs a different reading. A typical 6/8 measure contains six eighth-note units organized into two groups of three. The main pulse is usually two dotted-quarter beats, each dividing into three eighth notes. Count ONE-two-three FOUR-five-six to feel the groups, or use two larger pulses with three subdivisions each. Do not assume 6/8 is simply six equally strong beats. It has the same total eighth-note duration as 3/4, but the usual grouping differs: 6/8 is three plus three, while 3/4 is two plus two plus two. Listen for how the accents organize that shared total.
sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p2: Check a measure by adding its durations, including rests. In 4/4, two quarter notes plus one half note fill the bar. In 3/4, a dotted half note fills it. In 6/8, two dotted quarters do the same. A piece may begin with an incomplete pickup measure, so a short opening is not necessarily a printing mistake. Read the meter, look for repeated rhythmic groups, and count one complete measure before starting. When practicing with a metronome, decide which written note value the click represents; a number such as 80 is incomplete musical information without that beat-unit decision.
sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.title: Rests and dynamics
sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p0: A rest is a measured silence. It has a duration just like a sounding note, so you continue counting while not playing. Whole, half, quarter, eighth, and sixteenth rests correspond to those note values. A whole rest hangs below a staff line, while a half rest sits on a line. A whole-rest symbol may also indicate an entire measure of silence regardless of that measure's meter. Watch the context instead of assuming every whole-rest symbol always means exactly four quarter-note beats.
sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p1: For a simple exercise, alternate a quarter note and a quarter rest in 4/4. Play on one, stay silent on two, play on three, and stay silent on four. Keep your counting continuous and release the note when the rest begins. On a real piano, a held sustain pedal can blur the silence, so practice without it at first. A rest is an active part of the phrase: it can separate ideas, create anticipation, or leave room for another instrument.
sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p2: Dynamics describe relative loudness. Piano, written p, means soft; forte, f, means loud. Mezzo-piano and mezzo-forte, mp and mf, indicate moderately soft and moderately loud. These are musical relationships, not fixed volume measurements. A crescendo asks for increasing loudness and a diminuendo for decreasing loudness. On a physical keyboard, explore a comfortable range of touch without striking harshly. A basic virtual keyboard may play at a fixed level, so use the markings as reading practice even when the tool cannot reproduce every expressive nuance.
sf.editorial.guide.practice.title: A ten-minute reading routine
sf.editorial.guide.practice.p0: Spend the first two minutes locating a few anchor notes without guessing: middle C, treble G4, and bass F3. Say each name and find its key. Use minutes three and four for a small note drill in one clef, keeping the range narrow enough that you can explain your answers. If you miss a pitch, identify whether the error came from the clef, staff position, or octave. Write down one troublesome pair to revisit tomorrow. This makes your routine responsive to what you actually need rather than a fixed race to answer more questions.
sf.editorial.guide.practice.p1: During minutes five and six, clap a short rhythm and count aloud. During minutes seven and eight, combine that rhythm with a tiny melody. C–D–E–D–C is enough; you can also use a simple public-domain tune such as Hot Cross Buns or a beginner arrangement of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. Choose an arrangement whose range and rhythm match your current skill, because different versions can have very different difficulty. Read one measure ahead when possible, but stay slow enough to keep the pulse. If you lose your place, pause deliberately and restart from a clear point.
sf.editorial.guide.practice.p2: Use the final two minutes to play the short phrase again and notice one improvement and one next step. Perhaps the note names were faster but the rests still felt uncertain. Tomorrow, begin with that uncertainty. Short, regular sessions provide repeated chances to recall what you learned; long sessions are not a substitute for attention. When you are ready for a structured sequence, explore the piano lessons and continue using the free tools for focused review. Progress varies with experience and practice, so measure it by increasingly comfortable tasks rather than promising yourself a particular completion date.
sf.editorial.guide.faq.title: Common questions and your next step
sf.editorial.guide.faq.p0: How long does it take to read music? You can begin recognizing a few positions in a first session, but fluent reading develops through repeated practice with actual phrases. The timeline depends on the instrument, the music, and your prior experience. Aim first to read a small range accurately at a comfortable pace.
sf.editorial.guide.faq.p1: Do I need a teacher? You can learn basic symbols and practice recognition independently. A teacher can help with technique, listening, and habits that are hard to assess alone. These tools support practice, while your goals and the difficulties you encounter determine whether additional guidance would be useful.
sf.editorial.guide.faq.p2: Do I need a piano? A virtual keyboard is enough to connect early note names with sounds and staff positions. Learning to play an actual piano also requires touch, coordination, and comfortable movement, which an onscreen keyboard cannot fully teach. You can start reading before buying an instrument.
sf.editorial.guide.faq.p3: What should I do next? Return to the music notes trainer and try a small set without hints. Choose the treble or bass page for a focused review, or explore chords once single notes feel familiar. Keep this guide nearby and revisit the section that answers your next specific question.

sf.editorial.guide.rhythm-tip: Clap: half note → quarter note → two eighth notes. Count: ONE (hold two) THREE FOUR-and. The entire pattern fills one measure of 4/4.
sf.editorial.guide.source: Further reading: Open Music Theory on compound meter
sf.rhythm.title: Find your steady beat
sf.rhythm.intro: Start the metronome and clap once per click. Then use Tap on each beat to check your spacing. The higher click marks beat one.
sf.rhythm.tempoHelp: 40–160 BPM. Stop the metronome to change the tempo.
sf.rhythm.estimate: After two taps, the estimate compares your last 16 tap intervals with the selected beat length. It measures spacing, not alignment with the click. Browser and device timing can affect the result. Claps are not recorded.
sf.rhythm.audioError: Sound could not start. Try the Start button again and check your browser sound settings.
